author: Ethan's repotted moth orchid from Baraboo (photos of July 31, 2026)

plants.aliases: Baraboo orchid (from Ethan's mother's house in Baraboo, Wisconsin)
plants.location: At his mother's house in Baraboo, Wisconsin (last seen July 31, 2026, on a covered porch)
plants.container: Grey plastic pot with drainage holes (drilled July 31), almost entirely orchid bark, an old wooden flower stake with a clip
plants.id_basis: Broad, thick, glossy strap-shaped leaves in two opposite rows from a single short stem, and thick silver-green aerial roots with bright green growing tips: a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis). There is no tag and no flower in the photos, so the hybrid and its flower colour are not known. It came from Ethan's mother's house in Baraboo, Wisconsin.
plants.id_alternatives:
Phalaenopsis hybrid (store orchid)
Doritaenopsis (an older name for some hybrids)
plants.id_improve:
A photo of the flowers when it blooms (colour, size, markings)
Any tag or the receipt, if his mother has it
plants.temp_notes: Warm-growing. A few weeks of nights around 60 F in autumn set the flower spike; keep it above 55 F.
plants.humidity_notes: Likes humid air with movement; buds drop in very dry rooms.
plants.light_hours: 4-6 h bright indirect, or a grow light 10-12 h
plants.light_notes: Leaves should be a medium grass green: dark green means too little light, yellow-green or red-tinged means too much. Never hot midday sun.
plants.winter_summary: A tropical orchid: indoors all year in Round Rock.
plants.winter_triggers: Already indoors; away from cold glass and heater vents.
plants.winter_steps:
Cooler nights (60-65 F) for a few weeks in autumn help a flower spike form.
Water a little less in winter; let the bark dry between waterings.
Feed lightly or not at all until the spike shows.
plants.indoor_setup: East window or a grow light 12-18 in away. Humidity 50% or more; a small fan nearby helps. Water in the morning so the crown dries by night.
plants.health_summary: As of July 31, 2026 (Ethan has not seen it since). Repotted July 31: rotted roots removed, drainage holes added, healthy roots set into orchid bark. The leaves are firm and glossy with a reddish tint at the edges, and there are fresh green root tips, so it is putting out new roots. There is no flower spike and no keiki right now, and dried, browning leaf bases at the crown need watching for rot.
plants.health_observations:
Leaves broad, glossy and firm, with reddish edges (can mean strong light)
Fresh bright-green root tips after the repot
Healthy silver-green roots, most now in the bark; a few rest over the rim, which is normal
Rotted roots removed at the repot (July 31)
Dried, brown leaf bases at the crown beside the stake
No flower spike or keiki seen
The pot had no drainage holes until July 31
plants.health_steps:
It is a tropical orchid and this is Wisconsin: it must be indoors, in a bright window, well before nights fall below 55°F.
Water when the bark is dry and the roots look silver; water at the pot edge, not into the crown.
Blot any water out of the crown with a paper towel, and keep the leaf bases in the crown dry.
Let a few aerial roots stay in open air; do not bend or cram them into the bark.
Check the crown and the roots when next seen; trim dried leaf bases only once they come away easily.
Check whether the old flower spike is still green: a live node can grow a keiki, with keiki paste on it.
Put a saucer or catch pot under the pot, and empty it after watering.
plants.notes: It lives at Ethan's mother's house in Baraboo, Wisconsin, and Ethan has not seen it since July 31, 2026, so its health and spot here are as of then. Photographed July 31, 2026, before and after the repot. Identified from the photos alone. Moth orchids do not divide, so a keiki on an old flower spike is the way to propagate it.
plants.water_notes: Water when the roots in the pot turn silver and the bark is dry, roughly every 7-10 days: soak the pot for 10 minutes or run water through it, then drain fully. Never let water sit in the crown or in a cache pot. Firm roots and plump leaves say it is right; limp leaves say the roots are either dry or rotted.
plants.soil_medium: Medium orchid bark with a little charcoal and perlite, in a pot with large drainage holes (clear pots show the roots).
plants.fertilizer: Orchid feed at quarter strength with most waterings ("weakly, weekly"), plain water every fourth time
plants.pests_watch:
Mealybugs: white cottony fluff in the leaf axils and under the leaves
Scale: brown or white bumps on leaves and flower spikes
Spider mites: silvery pitting on the leaf undersides
plants.pest_steps:
Look into the leaf axils and along the leaf undersides every week.
Dab mealybugs with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud, then spray the whole plant (axils, undersides, the top of the medium) with insecticidal soap or 70% alcohol, repeating every 5-7 days for three weeks.
Keep an infested plant away from the others until clear for a month.
plants.growth_habit: A monopodial orchid: a short stem with a fan of thick, strap-shaped leaves, thick silver-green aerial roots, flowers on a spike from between the leaves
plants.height_pot: 6 to 12 in of leaves; a flower spike to 2 ft
plants.growth_rate: Slow (one or two leaves a year)
plants.native_range: Hybrids of Phalaenopsis species from South-East Asia, the Philippines and northern Australia, growing on trees in humid forest.
plants.bloom: A spike of long-lasting flowers (white, pink, purple, yellow or spotted) once or twice a year, usually winter to spring, each spike open for 2-3 months.
plants.propagation: Keikis (plantlets) that form on old flower spikes, potted up once they have roots 2-3 in long.

care.note: Removed the rotted roots, set the healthy aerial roots into the mix, drilled drainage holes in the grey pot; almost entirely orchid bark (Ethan, July 31)

pot_mix.notes: Almost entirely orchid bark; the rest is not recorded (Ethan, July 31); he does not know what else is in it. Grey pot with drainage holes added (no saucer in the after photos).

requests.text: Next time you see it, or ask your mother: where is it now (indoors, in a bright window?), is the old flower spike still green (a live node can grow a keiki), what else is in the bark mix, and has it flowered since July?
